sections.heading: Lead
Writing and composition
sections.wikitext:
The synth line was written circa 1981 by [[Eddie Van Halen]], but it was rejected by the other members of the band. In 1983, producer [[Ted Templeman]] asked Roth to listen to the unused song idea. Riding around in the back of his 1951 [[Mercury (automobile)|Mercury]], with band roadie Larry Hostler driving, Roth listened repeatedly to the tune. To come up with a lyric for it, he remembered seeing a TV news report the night before about a suicidal [[Jumper (person)|jumper]]. Roth thought that one of the onlookers at such an event would inevitably yell "go ahead and jump". Roth bounced this suggestion off Hostler who agreed it was good; however, instead of describing a potential suicide, the lyrics were written as an invitation to action, life and love. Roth later told [[Musician (magazine)|''Musician'']] magazine that Hostler was "probably the most responsible for how it came out."<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OyZyWKcmRhEC&pg=PT144 |page=144 |last=Crouse |first=Richard |title=Who Wrote The Book Of Love? |publisher=Doubleday Canada |year=2012 |isbn=9780385674423}}</ref> The song is set in the key of [[C major]], with the guitar solo in the key of [[B-flat minor|B♭ minor]]. "Jump" has a moderate [[common time]] [[tempo]] of 129 beats per minute.<ref>{{cite book|title=Van Halen Guitar Anthology|pages=148–53|publisher=Alfred|location=Van Nuys, California|year=2006|isbn=9780897246729|oclc=605214049}}</ref>

Ted Templeman recalls that "Jump" was recorded at Eddie Van Halen's newly constructed home studio. "Engineer [[Donn Landee]] and Ed put the track down alone in the middle of the night. We recut it once in one take for sonic reasons. Dave wrote the lyrics that afternoon in the backseat of his Mercury convertible. We finished all vocals that afternoon and mixed it that evening."<ref>Van Halen: A visual history: 1978-1984, Neil Zlozower, 2008</ref>

The keyboard part was performed on an [[Oberheim OB-Xa]].<ref>{{cite web|date=April 1, 2019|title=Hear David Lee Roth and Dutch DJ Armin Van Buuren's EDM Version of Van Halen's 'Jump'|url=https://www.guitarworld.com/news/hear-david-lee-roth-and-dutch-dj-armin-van-buurens-edm-version-of-van-halens-jump|access-date=June 24, 2019|website=[[Guitar World]]}}</ref> Live performances began with Eddie's [[synthesizer]] solo "1984". During the reunion tour with Roth, the two songs were used for the band's encore.

According to [[Daryl Hall]] of [[Hall & Oates]], "[Eddie] Van Halen told me that he copied the synth part from '[[Kiss on My List]]' and used it in 'Jump.' I don't have a problem with that at all."<ref>"[https://www.mixonline.com/recording/classic-tracks-hall-oates-i-cant-go-no-can-do-365614 Classic Tracks: Hall & Oates 'I Can't Go For That (No Can Do)']" {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060830062331/http://mixonline.com/mag/audio_hall_oates_cant/index.html |date=2006-08-30}}. mixonline.com, 2006.</ref>
[[File:Van Halen - Jump 2007-11-10.jpg|thumb|left|Van Halen performs "Jump", November 10, 2007.|200px]]
Musically, the song was a departure from the band's original style,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Prown |first1=Pete |author-link=Pete Prown |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=60Jde3l7WNwC&pg=PA165 |title=Legends of Rock Guitar: The Essential Reference of Rock's Greatest Guitarists |last2=Newquist |first2=HP |author-link2=HP Newquist |date=1997 |publisher=Hal Leonard |isbn=9780793540426 |page=165}}</ref> embracing more of a popular and radio-friendly sound. "Jump" has been described as a "[[synth-rock]]er",<ref>{{cite web|last=Jackson|first=Josh|date=February 1, 2012|title=The 80 Best Albums of the 1980s|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/1980s/best-albums-of-the-1980s/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204204840/https://www.pastemagazine.com/blogs/lists/2012/02/the-80-best-albums-of-the-1980s.html?p=5|archive-date=February 4, 2012|access-date=September 28, 2019|website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref> as a combination of hard rock and [[Popular music|pop]],<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WZ87AQAAIAAJ|title=Musicians and Composers of the 20th Century|last=Cramer|first=Alfred William|date=2009|publisher=Salem Press|isbn=9781587655173|page=1540|quote=In 1984 the song 'Jump' reached number one on the Billboard charts. The radio-friendly song combined hard rock with synthesizer-driven pop music.}}</ref> as exemplifying [[pop rock]] of the 1980s, built on a classic [[Rock music|rock]] foundation of repeated bass notes and having standard rock instrumentation,<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nIZSM3zxNUEC&pg=PA305 |page=305 |last=Campbell |first=Michael |title=Popular Music in America: And The Beat Goes On |date=2008 |publisher=Cengage Learning |isbn=9780495505303 |edition=3}}</ref> and as "a true rock masterpiece."<ref name=Sumrall1994>{{cite book |date=1994 |last=Sumrall |first=Harry |title=Pioneers of Rock and Roll: 100 artists who changed the face of rock |publisher=Billboard Books |page=[https://archive.org/details/pioneersofrockro0000sumr/page/274 274] |isbn=9780823076284 |url=https://archive.org/details/pioneersofrockro0000sumr/page/274}}</ref> The song has been also described as a [[Pop metal|pop]]/[[glam metal]] anthem.<ref>{{cite book|last=Popoff|first=Martin|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rfNzBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA58|title=The Big Book of Hair Metal|publisher=Voyageur Press|year=2014|isbn=9781627883757|page=58}}</ref><ref Zaleski|date=October 7, 2020|title=Eddie Van Halen: 10 of his best songs|url=http://www.theguardian.com/music/2020/oct/07/eddie-van-halen-10-of-his-best-songs|access-date=April 11, 2021|website=[[The The synth line was written circa 1981 by Eddie Van Halen, but it was rejected by the other members of the band. In 1983, producer Ted Templeman asked Roth to listen to the unused song idea. Riding around in the back of his 1951 Mercury, with band roadie Larry Hostler driving, Roth listened repeatedly to the tune. To come up with a lyric for it, he remembered seeing a TV news report the night before about a suicidal jumper. Roth thought that one of the onlookers at such an event would inevitably yell "go ahead and jump". Roth bounced this suggestion off Hostler who agreed it was good; however, instead of describing a potential suicide, the lyrics were written as an invitation to action, life and love. Roth later told Musician magazine that Hostler was "probably the most responsible for how it came out." The song is set in the key of C major, with the guitar solo in the key of B♭ minor. "Jump" has a moderate common time tempo of 129 beats per minute.

Ted Templeman recalls that "Jump" was recorded at Eddie Van Halen's newly constructed home studio. "Engineer Donn Landee and Ed put the track down alone in the middle of the night. We recut it once in one take for sonic reasons. Dave wrote the lyrics that afternoon in the backseat of his Mercury convertible. We finished all vocals that afternoon and mixed it that evening."

The keyboard part was performed on an Oberheim OB-Xa. Live performances began with Eddie's synthesizer solo "1984". During the reunion tour with Roth, the two songs were used for the band's encore.

According to Daryl Hall of Hall & Oates, "[Eddie] Van Halen told me that he copied the synth part from 'Kiss on My List' and used it in 'Jump.' I don't have a problem with that at all."
thumb|left|Van Halen performs "Jump", November 10, 2007.|200px
Musically, the song was a departure from the band's original style, embracing more of a popular and radio-friendly sound. "Jump" has been described as a "synth-rocker", as a combination of hard rock and pop, as exemplifying pop rock of the 1980s, built on a classic rock foundation of repeated bass notes and having standard rock instrumentation, and as "a true rock masterpiece." The song has been also described as a pop/glam metal anthem.

sections.heading: Music video
Sporting anthem
sections.wikitext:
Since December 1986, before every home game at the [[Stade Vélodrome]], [[Olympique de Marseille]] football players enter to Van Halen's song.<ref>{{cite web |title=French football team unveils Eddie Van Halen tribute |url=https://www.vhnd.com/2020/10/20/french-football-team-unveils-eddie-van-halen-tribute/ |access-date=October 20, 2020 |website=vhnd.com|date=October 20, 2020 }}</ref>

As part of the [[goal celebration]]s it is also played every time [[A.C. Milan]] scores a goal at their home ground [[San Siro]].<ref>{{cite news |title=The songs of soccer, from stadium anthems to Ronaldo's solo |url=https://www.dw.com/en/the-songs-of-soccer-from-stadium-anthems-to-ronaldos-solo/a-19313958 |access-date=October 9, 2018 |agency=DW.com}}</ref>
 
The song is a staple at [[Detroit Pistons]] [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] games whenever a jump ball is called.

The original [[Winnipeg Jets (1972–96)|Winnipeg Jets]] of the [[National Hockey League]] played "Jump" on the arena PA system as the team came onto the ice. They used the song until the team's departure for Phoenix after the 1995–96 season. On the team's [[Winnipeg Jets|return in 2011]], public outcry for use of the song initially was ignored, as the team's management company [[True North Sports and Entertainment]] wished to create a break with the past, considering the previous Jets a different organization from the new Jets (the former [[Atlanta Thrashers]]). However, in 2016 True North resumed the use of "Jump", this time as the team's [[goal song]] whenever the Jets score a goal at [[Bell MTS Place]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Minuk |first=David |title=Winnipeg Jets pick Jump by Van Halen as new goal song |url=https://illegalcurve.com/winnipeg-jets-pick-jump-by-van-halen-as-new-goal-song/ |website=Illegal Curve |date=October 14, 2016 |access-date=December 5, 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220095057/http://illegalcurve.com/2016/10/14/winnipeg-jets-pick-jump-by-van-halen-as-new-goal-song/ |archive-date=December 20, 2016}}</ref>

"Jump" was the theme song for the introduction of [[Chicago Cubs]] broadcasts on [[WGN-TV]] in 1984 and 1985, and was formerly what the team would run onto the field to before the top of the 1st inning.<ref>{{cite news|last=Hawley|first=Larry|title=Van Halen's 'Jump' has a special meaning for the Cubs and their WGN-TV broadcasts|url=https://wgntv.com/sports/cubs/van-halens-jump-has-a-special-meaning-for-the-cubs-and-their-wgn-tv-broadcasts/|publisher=Nexstar Inc.|website=WGNTV.com|date=October 7, 2020|access-date=October 15, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=NBC Sports Bay Area Staff|title=Nine best Van Halen sports anthems ranked, in Eddie's memory|url=https://www.nbcsports.com/bayarea/nine-eddie-van-halen-songs-became-sports-anthems-pumped-fans?cid=Yahoo&partner=ya4nbcs|publisher=Comcast SportsNet California, LLC|website=NBCSports.com|date=October 6, 2020|access-date=October 15, 2020}}</ref>

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext: Upon its release, the UK publication ''[[Music Week]]'' felt that "Jump" catered to American sensibilities and characterized the song as "synthesizer pomp rock" with a "polite" vocal delivery from Roth.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=January 21, 1984 |title=Select Singles |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1984/Music-Week-1984-01-21.pdf |access-date=September 1, 2025 |magazine=[[Music Week]] |page=44 |via=World Radio History}}</ref>  "Jump" was ranked number 15 on [[VH1]]'s 100 Greatest Songs of the 1980s. The song was listed by [[The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum]] as one of the "500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll."<ref>"[http://www.rockhall.com/exhibithighlights/500-songs 500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll]" {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070502032502/http://www.rockhall.com/exhibithighlights/500-songs |date=May 2, 2007}}. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum, 2007.</ref> Chuck Klosterman of [[Vulture.com]] ranked it the 16th-best Van Halen song, calling it "an articulation of unadulterated joy and the unprecedented power of six rudimentary keyboard chords arranged in the best possible sequence."<ref name="vulture"/> Ahead of the [[2012 Summer Olympics]], the song was voted as the favourite sporting anthem, in a poll of members of [[PRS for Music]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nme.com/news/music/van-halen-7-1262236|title=Van Halen's 'Jump' voted most popular sporting song|website=NME|first=Leonie|last=Cooper|date=July 26, 2012|access-date=October 24, 2020}}</ref>
sections.text: Upon its release, the UK publication Music Week felt that "Jump" catered to American sensibilities and characterized the song as "synthesizer pomp rock" with a "polite" vocal delivery from Roth.  "Jump" was ranked number 15 on VH1's 100 Greatest Songs of the 1980s. The song was listed by The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum as one of the "500 Songs that Shaped Rock and Roll." Chuck Klosterman of Vulture.com ranked it the 16th-best Van Halen song, calling it "an articulation of unadulterated joy and the unprecedented power of six rudimentary keyboard chords arranged in the best possible sequence." Ahead of the 2012 Summer Olympics, the song was voted as the favourite sporting anthem, in a poll of members of PRS for Music.

sections.wikitext: "Jump" was nominated at the 27th Annual Grammy Awards (1984) in the "Best Rock Performance By a Duo or Group with Vocal" category, losing to ''[[Purple Rain (album)|Purple Rain]]'' by [[Prince (musician)|Prince & The Revolution]].<ref>{{cite web |title=GRAMMY Awards - Van Halen |url=https://www.grammy.com/artists/van-halen/8408 |access-date=October 11, 2020 |website=[[Grammy.com]]}}</ref>

sections.wikitext: Dutch DJ [[Armin van Buuren]] debuted his own private remix of "Jump" at the 2019 Miami [[Ultra Music Festival]] with David Lee Roth on stage.<ref>{{cite news |title=David Lee Roth Joins Armin van Buuren for 'Jump' at 2019 Ultra Music Festival |url=https://loudwire.com/david-lee-roth-armin-van-buuren-jump-2019-ultra-music-festival/ |access-date=February 3, 2020 |agency=Loudwire}}</ref> This remix was released through [[Big Beat Records (American record label)|Big Beat Records]] on May 17, 2019.<ref>[https://www.beatport.com/track/jump-armin-van-buuren-extended-mix/11923727 Jump (Armin van Buuren Extended Mix) by Van Halen] at Beatport</ref>

"Live: Jump" was released as a single in 1993. The performance was recorded at the [[Selland Arena]] in [[Fresno, California]], in May 1992, during the [[For Unlawful Carnal Knowledge Tour]]. "Jump" and the B-side, "[[Love Walks In]]", are the same versions that appear on the album ''[[Live: Right Here, Right Now]]''. On the [[compact disc]] release of the single, "[[OU812|Mine All Mine]]" and "[[Eagles Fly]]" are previously unreleased live versions. All songs were produced by Van Halen and [[Andy Johns]], except "Mine All Mine", which was produced by Van Halen and [[Donn Landee]].<ref>{{cite AV media notes|title=Live: Jump |others=Van Halen|year=1993|publisher=Warner Bros. Records Inc.|id=W0155CD|location=Germany}}</ref>
